title: TB1-11518
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXX, the claimant, is a citizen of Pakistan. He claims protection under ss. 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS (From PIF Narrative)

The claimant's father lived in USA the past few years. Because of this and the fact that he is thought to have money, his family was targeted in Pakistan. Phone calls were made to his mother, which caused the claimant to leave school. On several occasions men beat the claimant, demanded money from the claimant's father and threatened to kidnap the claimant. No action was taken when the authorities were reported to.
Thus, the claimant's family arranged to have the claimant go to USA, but they were stopped in Canada, so that is why he made a refugee claim. He fears kidnapping, especially because he is a boy.

The Panel finds the claimant to not be a Convention refugee under Section 96 of the IRPA, as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Pakistan on any of the five Convention grounds. The Panel also finds that the claimant is not a person in need of protection under Section 97 of the IRPA, as, on a balance of probabilities, his removal to Pakistan would not subject him personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. The Panel's reasons are as follows.

The claimant's personal identity and his identity as a citizen of Pakistan have been established by a copy of the claimant's birth certificate in Exhibit C-7, as well as the USA immigration information in Exhibit C-3.

The Panel has considered all of the evidence and the counsel's written post-hearing submission dated April 11, 2012. This is a very unusual refugee claim, and was very hard to determine. The claimant is an 11 year old boy from Pakistan, and his story may be seen as a sad one. Apparently, his parents are not together, his father having gone to live in USA. The mother still lives in a house in Pakistan, with one other sibling of the claimant. Several of the children went to live with the father in USA. The claimant was also the subject of a sponsorship to USA by the father, but for unknown reasons it did not succeed or go forward, apparently. The Panel incidentally notes that this indicates a pre-existing intention on the part of the father to have the claimant leave Pakistan, independent of any reason related to fear of kidnappings.

The father is in trouble with the law in USA, having been charged with some drug charge. It appears serious enough so that he had to surrender his passport, and cannot leave USA. He thus gave evidence by telephone at the hearing. The minor did not testify, and in fact left the hearing room after being ID'd.

The father is apparently involved with another woman. The claimant was apparently given to this woman, and the woman attempted to smuggle herself and the claimant to USA, to the father. For reasons which could not be explained, they attempted to fly to USA through Canada, but got arrested here. The woman is apparently in USA with the father, and the child was left here in the care of the Peel Childrens' Aid Society (CAS). Peel Region is where Toronto Airport principally is, so they took jurisdiction.

The wheels of social service took over. A Designated Representative (DR) was appointed, from a prominent Toronto law firm, which helpfully assists this Board from time to time on these matters. The Panel thanks the DR and his firm again, as it did at the hearing. The CAS representative took some control over the claimant, who is now living in a foster home. Both the CAS rep. and the DR were present at the hearing, and gave some testimony.

After a while, it was apparently decided by the DR and CAS that a refugee claim should be made, and it was. This decision was made when the DR learned that such a claim had to be made before the hearing before an Immigration Division Member, otherwise it would be barred thereafter. Thus, it was done, to avoid deportation. Present counsel was appointed, a prominent refugee lawyer known to the Panel, and the Panel thanks him for his assistance as well. It is thus noted that the claimant was not sent to Canada, or USA, to make a refugee claim - it was more of an "accidental" claim. The intention was for the claimant to simply live illegally with his father in USA.

The PIF Narrative was prepared by counsel, in conjunction with the DR. He got his information principally from the father in USA. However, as the key events allegedly took place in Pakistan, and the father was not there, but in USA, apparently the information in the Narrative came from the mother, as relayed to the father.

As such, gauging of credibility was problematic. The Panel assumes that the DR and CAS, as well as of course counsel, faithfully provided information to the Board as relayed to them. There are serious credibility concerns, and the author of the Narrative, and the person ultimately most responsible for providing the allegations, is the father. Fortunately, the Panel had an opportunity to orally examine the father, although in a limited fashion because it was only by telephone, not even by videoconference.

Even with all these challenges, the Panel did have to gauge credibility. In addition, the Panel examined whether the claimant, by virtue of his status as a young boy of a father living in USA who has some wealth, would be subject to persecution, even if his specific allegations were rejected, which they were, below.

In the PIF Narrative it was written, in the person of the claimant, that he was beaten by men when they approached him near his house. The father was asked to confirm that the claimant was beaten, and he said he was not. It was pointed out to him that he had indicated in the Narrative that he was. The father attempted to explain this by saying that he was not there, but he was told that men tried to attack the claimant.

The Panel unfortunately cannot accept these explanations. The father may not have been there, but the Narrative came from him, and he was testifying, and the versions were inconsistent. Also, he was unable to explain the inconsistency, and from it the Panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

Counsel questioned the DR on this issue. The DR said the claimant told him that there was an attempted abduction, in which the claimant was grabbed and injured, but the DR did not recall the claimant using the word "beat" or "beaten." The DR suggested, though, that it might have been him who conveyed to counsel, when counsel was preparing the PIF, that the claimant had been beaten. The Panel appreciates the DR's efforts to clarify the situation, but it really was not clarified. Given the other concerns in regard to credibility, the Panel still makes a negative inference as to credibility from this inconsistency.

It was written in the Narrative that these men demanded money from the father, through the claimant. The father was asked to confirm this, and he said, no, the money was demanded from the claimant's mother. He was asked why he had written, then, that the money was demanded from him, and he said it is obvious that the mother would have to provide the money. It would be obvious if the Panel accepted that these men knew the father was away and targeted the family in his absence, but the Panel does not accept this. As such, from this inconsistency the Panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

The father was asked if the police were ever informed about the alleged approaches / beatings on the claimant. He said yes, his wife informed the police. However, he was not able to supply any police report in regard to what would appear to be the most serious contact with these men, when the claimant was allegedly physically confronted / beaten. He did supply police reports in regard to alleged threatening phone calls. In addition, he could supply no medical report in connection with the claimant being beaten, if he was beaten.

The alleged events of XXX, 2011 were discussed. The father said the claimant was attacked, and his wife reported it to the police. However, Exhibits C-6 and C-9, referring to the XXX, 2011 events, only refer to telephone calls, and not attacks. Unfortunately the father was not questioned as to this inconsistency, so the Panel does not make a negative inference as to credibility therefrom.

These exhibits indicate the threatening phone calls to have been reported on XXXX, 2011. It is also noted that the claimant flew out of Pakistan for Canada three days later, on XXXX, 2011. The father indicated that it was he who bought the airline tickets, and he believes he would have done so about ten days before departure, or before the alleged report to the police on XXXX, 2011. The father was asked why his wife would bother making reports to the police that their son was being threatened, if his departure for Canada was already planned by that time. All he could say was that he had no clue, and it was required to report. Then he said that it was required to wait a few days before reporting to the police. Both of these statements appear inaccurate and also not to the point, so the claimant could not explain why a detailed police report would be made, if firm plans were already underway to have the claimant leave Pakistan anyway.

This is a factor in the Panel's finding that the police reports are not genuine. In addition, two of them are handwritten. The father was asked why this would be so, and he said it is a primitive part of Pakistan, and the police don't have electricity, and they used carbon paper to duplicate the police reports. The Panel finds it hard to believe that the police can operate with no electricity, and the Panel also notes no telltale imprints of carbon copy use on any of the three police reports, such as deep imprint. In fact, Exhibit C-6, allegedly an Interrogation Report from XXXX 2011, by the same police, is in fact a photocopy of what appears to be typewritten text, so it would appear as if electricity must have been used to make this copy. The Panel retained the originals thereof in the file for genuineness assessment purposes, as the marked exhibits themselves, and would have no objection to counsel being provided with the original exhibits upon request post-hearing, should he so desire.

The father was asked if he could provide the envelope in which the police reports were allegedly delivered from Pakistan. He said he thought he could provide it, as it came by courier from Pakistan, sent by his brother. However, no such envelope was provided to the Panel with counsel's post-hearing submission, even though it was identified as important and indicated to have likely been able to have been made available.
The claimant was unable to explain why none of the police reports were on letterhead - he just said there was no log book, which does not explain anything.

The DR testified that he got the police reports from Customs in Canada, or from the CAS rep., he was not sure. The CAS rep. was questioned as to where the police reports came from, and she said she got them from the father in USA. She was specifically asked if she had the envelope in which the documents came, and she said she did, but not at the hearing. Again, no such envelope was provided to the Panel with counsel's post-hearing submission, even though it was identified as important and indicated to have likely been able to have been made available.

The Panel wishes to make clear that it in no way wishes to impeach any of the testimony or efforts of the DR or CAS. The Panel must note, though, that, even though the envelope was identified as important at the hearing, and in fact it was indicated by the CAS rep. that it was in her possession, it was not provided to the Panel.

Thus, considering the above as well as noting the other credibility concerns in this claim, the Panel finds these police reports to be not genuine, and from this finding the Panel makes a negative inference as to credibility. Further, the Panel is entitled to make a general negative inference as to credibility from the provision of false documents, and it does so. In this regard, the Panel notes that this finding is consistent with Item 3.3 of Exhibit R/A-1, which speaks of the proliferation of false documents emanating from Pakistan. The Panel additionally notes that counsel himself apparently generally inferred the proliferation of false documents emanating from Pakistan in his post-hearing submission, although in the Identity segment of his submission (which is not to suggest that counsel necessarily agrees that these documents are not genuine).

The CAS rep. was also questioned, as indicated. She testified that she spoke to the claimant's mother in Pakistan, who told her that the claimant was taken away by kidnappers, and thereafter returned by them. She also said that the claimant himself told her that he had actually been abducted, but that he ran away. She was asked why, if the claimant had actually been abducted, this did not appear in the PIF Narrative. At this point the DR jumped in to answer. He explained this by saying that the Narrative was referring to the incident when there was an attempted abduction, and force was exerted on the claimant. However, this would not appear to be correct, as it was previously indicated that the claimant was actually abducted, and escaped. As well, as indicated above, this entire incident was not even mentioned in the Narrative. The CAS rep. then jumped in and retracted her statement that she heard that the claimant was actually kidnapped, and corrected it to it being an attempted abduction only. The Panel will refrain from making negative inferences from the laudable efforts of the DR and CAS on behalf of this innocent 11 year old, but must say that inconsistencies are evident from this evidence, so the Panel must give it little weight.

Considering all the above credibility issues, the Panel finds that the claimant's evidence, through his father, overall, has not been credible, and is insufficient to support the claimant's claim for refugee protection.

The Panel will now consider whether the claimant is likely to be kidnapped, having rejected the allegations about what happened to him in Pakistan. Documents were provided by counsel to show the father has moderate assets in USA, although by no means would he be deemed very wealthy. Perhaps, though, if Pakistan is quite poor, then even this middling wealth could be perceived as great wealth in Pakistan. The Panel will also assume that somehow, people in Pakistan, and even Taliban in Afghanistan, could come to know that this little boy living with his mother has a rich father in USA.

In this regard, as suggested by counsel in his submission, the Panel examined Exhibit C-4. The documentation there indicates that it is a significant problem, as per the Tribune article, in the "mid to high hundreds each year." That is, less than a thousand. Pakistan has a population of well over a hundred million people, and evidently tens of millions will be children. The Panel thus finds that there is a possibility of this occurring to the claimant, but it is only a mere possibility. That it, it does not rise to the level of a serious possibility. Thus, this aspect of the claimant is dismissed as well.

For the foregoing reasons, the Panel finds the claimant to not be a Convention refugee under s. 96, nor a person in need of protection under s. 97 of the IRPA. For these reasons, the claim is rejected. (signed) "M. Sterlin" M.
